title: Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a durable ability to repair ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in the epidermis well enough to substantially prevent the skin cancers that would otherwise arise from that damage. One route would restore or increase nucleotide excision repair, the cellular machinery that recognizes damaged DNA, removes the affected segment and replaces it. Another would provide an equivalent way to remove ultraviolet photoproducts before they become mutations. The defining achievement would be sustained clinical cancer prevention, rather than a short-lived improvement in a laboratory measure of DNA damage.

As a proposed scope, the intervention must protect the cells that can initiate the cancers being claimed. Prevention of keratinocyte cancers would require effective repair in the relevant keratinocyte populations; a melanoma-prevention claim would additionally require protection of melanocytes. Restoring a defective repair pathway and increasing protection in skin with ordinarily functioning repair are distinct applications, each requiring evidence. The concept does not assume that either application has been achieved.

significance.text: Xeroderma pigmentosum, or XP, illustrates the clinical importance of handling ultraviolet DNA damage. The reviewed 2012 article reports that XP patients under age 20 have approximately 10,000-fold higher non-melanoma skin cancer frequency and 2,000-fold higher melanoma frequency than the general population. These are age-specific comparisons reported by that review, rather than estimates for every person with XP. The article links unrepaired ultraviolet photoproducts to mutations and cancer, providing a strong biological rationale for prevention through repair.

If durable repair reduced new ultraviolet mutations enough to substantially prevent cancers, it could greatly reduce the burden of repeated tumors and treatment in susceptible patients. This would make repair a sustained preventive capability with consequences beyond transient reductions in DNA lesions. Extension to normally repaired but heavily exposed skin could have broader public-health importance, but benefit in that population cannot be inferred from correcting a severe inherited defect.

The biological analogy has important limits. XP is heterogeneous: the reviewed article states that XP variant has normal nucleotide excision repair and a different defect in tolerating DNA damage. Restoring nucleotide excision repair alone therefore would not address every XP mechanism. Equivalent photoproduct removal might still help, but that would require demonstration. Preventing new mutations also would not by itself remove established mutant clones or prevent cancers driven by other mechanisms.

As a mechanistic distinction, vaccination would seek protection through an immune response, whereas this concept seeks protection by preventing mutagenic DNA damage from persisting. The supplied evidence does not establish a universal skin-cancer vaccine as an available alternative. Nor does it justify saying that sunscreen or nicotinamide can have consequences only while being used: ongoing protection and the later consequences of damage already prevented are different questions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing demonstration is repair or equivalent photoproduct removal that is sufficiently effective and durable to substantially prevent ultraviolet-driven cancers. Historical evidence of benefit from a topical repair enzyme makes this a question of the magnitude, mechanism and persistence of prevention, rather than an absence of all clinical activity. The supplied evidence does not establish normalization of cancer risk, and it does not establish the concept's availability or unavailability as of November 1, 2026.

Engineering requirements inferred from the proposed goal include delivering an active intervention to the relevant epidermal cells, maintaining sufficient activity despite epidermal turnover and repeated ultraviolet exposure, and removing lesions before they become fixed mutations. A durable gene-based approach would need persistent correction or expression in the appropriate cell compartment. An enzyme-based approach would need an effective delivery and dosing strategy. These are requirements to demonstrate, not evidence that all topical bacterial enzymes necessarily penetrate poorly or act only transiently.

Further scientific barriers include matching treatment to the underlying repair defect, establishing adequate protection in melanocytes if melanoma prevention is claimed, and distinguishing prevention of new damage from the continuing effects of mutations already present. Safety and clinical benefit would need to hold over the intended treatment period. The supplied review does not establish current regulatory approval status for XP gene replacement, so absence of an approved skin therapy cannot be asserted from this package.

current_state.text: The full 2012 review, identified in the supplied evidence review as Shining a Light on Xeroderma Pigmentosum, reports a double-blind study of topical liposomal T4 endonuclease V in 20 XP patients that lowered rates of actinic keratoses and basal cell carcinoma. This is relevant historical clinical evidence for an externally supplied bacterial repair enzyme. It does not establish restoration of endogenous nucleotide excision repair, prevention of melanoma, durable normalization of cancer risk or applicability to normally repaired skin. The supplied review account gives no effect size or follow-up duration for this study.

The reconciled research attributes to a New England Journal of Medicine trial dated October 22, 2015 a 23 percent reduction in new non-melanoma skin cancers during 12 months of oral nicotinamide in high-risk patients, with no evidence of benefit after discontinuation. Those quantitative and follow-up claims are retained here as reports from the research notes: the trial text was not captured, and the supplied evidence review could not verify them. Even if confirmed, this would describe chemoprevention under the trial's conditions; it would not by itself demonstrate durable prevention through restored nucleotide excision repair.

The research notes attribute to a review dated June 28, 2024 a reduction in cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers after a single ultraviolet exposure when photolyase was combined with sunscreen. They also report that none of the treatments discussed returned human-skin dimer levels to baseline. The source text is absent from the retained evidence, so these findings and their experimental scope remain unverified here. A single-exposure photoproduct result, if confirmed, would support an enabling mechanism without establishing sustained cancer prevention.

The research describes a systematic review dated November 1, 2025 as finding signals of fewer lesions with repair-enzyme preparations, together with high risk of bias and heterogeneity that prevented a firm cancer-prevention conclusion. The research's access was described as a publisher extract, and no extract or full text was retained for the evidence review. Its findings therefore remain a provisional account, with uncertainty about the included interventions, endpoints and strength of evidence. Missing source text is not evidence that the reported findings are false.

The research also describes an NIH project as active in fiscal year 2025, developing an AAV vector carrying ERCC5 for xeroderma pigmentosum–Cockayne syndrome, with a neurological emphasis and further development needed before human trials. The retained NIH page contained only a short RePORTER shell. It could not substantiate the project identity, vector, indication, fiscal-year activity or developmental stage. These details remain unverified, and the cited project cannot establish a clinical skin-cancer prevention result.

Evidence-package synthesis: the supplied materials establish a biological rationale and historical clinical enzyme benefit, but do not establish the proposed durable preventive capability. They also do not support a comprehensive statement that no relevant clinical result exists as of November 1, 2026: the supplied search record is empty, and the newer cited sources were not available in substantive retained form. Present-day clinical and regulatory status remains unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: a controlled, multi-year study would show substantially fewer new ultraviolet-driven cancers in a clearly defined high-risk population. A repair-deficient cohort would directly test correction of defective repair; immunosuppressed organ-transplant recipients are another proposed population, with a different risk context. The protocol could pre-specify an ambitious benchmark in which treated incidence approaches that of a clearly defined, matched lower-risk population. Treatment benefit would require an appropriate controlled comparison, with ultraviolet exposure, surveillance and concurrent prevention measures accounted for. These are proposed design choices, not established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled multi-year reduction in ultraviolet-driven cancers in high-risk patients

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic demonstration: serial sampling would show fewer newly accumulating ultraviolet-signature mutations, alongside evidence that the intervention reaches and repairs damage in the relevant cell populations. A melanoma claim would require melanocyte coverage and adequately assessed melanoma outcomes; fewer keratinocyte cancers would not establish that claim. Mutation measurements would support the causal explanation, while reductions in dimers or actinic keratoses over months would remain insufficient substitutes for cancer-incidence evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Repair reaches relevant cells and reduces accumulating ultraviolet-signature mutations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: benefit should be reproduced in independent cohorts or settings, with adequate follow-up to characterize safety, persistence and any maintenance dosing required. Studies should distinguish prevention in treated skin from effects elsewhere, and specify the repair defect, cancer types, exposure conditions and baseline disease burden studied. If persistence after treatment cessation is claimed, that persistence must be measured. Successful finite studies would establish the demonstrated breadth of prevention, not universal protection across all skin cancers or patients.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduced prevention with characterized safety, persistence and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: DER-02, One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment, could overlap directly if durable repair were achieved by correcting an inherited defect in epidermal stem cells. DER-05 is defined by prevention of ultraviolet-driven cancer and also permits non-genomic repair approaches. DER-04, Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum, could supply a delivery capability, but passage through the barrier alone would not establish intracellular repair or clinical prevention.

Roster-based comparison: DER-06, Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field, is the closest complementary concept. Its title suggests action on a field in which mutations already exist, whereas DER-05 focuses on preventing new mutations through repair. That distinction is useful, but the supplied roster contains no detailed DER-06 mechanism, so clearance of existing clones cannot be treated as its verified specification. The entries remain distinct even if a future intervention combines both functions.

Roster-based comparison: DER-01, Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ, concerns broader organ restoration; restored skin could still require protection from ultraviolet damage. DER-08, Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone, shares a pigment-cell connection but concerns rebuilding a cell reservoir. DER-05 would need to protect melanocytes if it claimed melanoma prevention, without necessarily regenerating that reservoir.

Roster-based comparison: DER-03, Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory, and DER-07, A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march, concern immune or inflammatory outcomes rather than repair of ultraviolet DNA lesions. DER-09, Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated, and DER-10, In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars, concern wound and scar outcomes. Their shared dermatological setting does not make their defining endpoints equivalent to cancer prevention through DNA repair.

unresolved_issues: The 2015 nicotinamide trial text is absent; its reported effect size, follow-up findings and exact population remain unverified within this package.
The 2024 photolyase review and 2025 systematic review require substantive source text to resolve experimental scope, endpoints, effect sizes and methodological limitations.
The NIH page shell cannot verify the reported ERCC5/AAV project details, developmental stage or fiscal-year activity.
Clinical availability, regulatory approval status and relevant developments through November 1, 2026 remain unresolved because the supplied search record is empty.
The historical enzyme trial's effect size, follow-up duration and implications for persistent risk reduction are not established by the supplied review account.
The effective delivery strategy, relevant cell coverage, required repair activity and achievable duration remain open engineering questions.
Whether benefit can extend to normally repaired skin, XP variant or immunosuppressed transplant recipients requires separate demonstration.
The detailed scope of DER-06 is not supplied; its relationship to existing-clone clearance remains a roster-based interpretation.

The review's suggested omission of unverified newer-result details was not adopted in full: those details were retained as explicitly qualified research reports to preserve useful information from both inputs without asserting verification.

brief.title: Lasting skin repair that prevents sun-driven cancer
possible: People at high risk of skin cancer could gain lasting protection by repairing sunlight damage to DNA, their cells’ genetic material, before it becomes permanent mutations. Treatment would keep working in the skin’s outer layer well enough to substantially prevent cancers.
why: For people who repeatedly develop skin tumors, sustained prevention could mean fewer cancers and fewer treatments. Xeroderma pigmentosum, or XP, an inherited disorder affecting how cells handle DNA damage, shows how much cancer risk can rise when this protection fails.

sources.who: John J DiGiovanna and Kenneth H Kraemer
sources.showed: Their review links defective DNA repair in XP to sun-driven mutations and cancer. It also reports a trial in 20 patients where a skin-applied repair enzyme, a protein that acts on damaged DNA, reduced precancerous growths and basal cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer.
sources.quote: XP cells are hypersensitive to killing by UV and XP cancers have characteristic “UV signature” mutations.
sources.cited_for: The review supports the biological case for repair and reports clinical benefit from an externally supplied repair enzyme.
sources.not_established: The reported benefit does not establish lasting normalization of cancer risk or protection against melanoma.

sources.showed: This is a clinical trial of oral nicotinamide for skin-cancer prevention in high-risk patients.
sources.cited_for: The trial concerns drug-based prevention in people at high risk of skin cancer.
sources.not_established: Drug-based prevention alone does not demonstrate lasting protection through restored DNA repair.

sources.showed: This is a review discussing photolyase, a DNA-repair enzyme, combined with sunscreen and its effects on damage after ultraviolet exposure.
sources.cited_for: The review concerns removal of DNA damage caused by ultraviolet radiation, the damaging component of sunlight.
sources.not_established: Less DNA damage after an exposure does not establish sustained cancer prevention.

sources.showed: This is a systematic review bringing together studies of repair-enzyme preparations and their effects on skin lesions.
sources.cited_for: The review concerns whether repair-enzyme preparations reduce skin lesions.
sources.not_established: Bias and differences between studies prevent a firm conclusion about cancer prevention.

sources.showed: This is a gene-delivery development project for an inherited DNA-repair disorder, with an emphasis on neurological disease.
sources.cited_for: The project concerns a possible route to replacing a faulty DNA-repair gene.
sources.not_established: Developing gene delivery does not establish prevention of skin cancer in people.

shown: The clearest clinical foothold is the small XP trial described by DiGiovanna and Kraemer. A skin-applied bacterial repair enzyme lowered rates of precancerous growths and basal cell skin cancers. That establishes some clinical benefit from added repair activity.
missing: A controlled study lasting years would need to demonstrate substantial cancer prevention through sustained repair.
Treatment would need to reach the cells that start the cancers and remain effective as skin renews and sunlight exposure continues.
Protection against melanoma, a cancer arising in pigment-producing cells, would require repair in those cells and fewer melanoma cases.

milestones.label: Fewer sun-driven cancers over years in high-risk patients
milestones.explanation: A controlled study lasting years would have to find substantially fewer new sun-driven cancers in a defined high-risk group. This would establish the clinical prevention that improved DNA-damage measurements alone cannot prove.

milestones.label: Repair reaches cancer-starting cells and reduces new mutations
milestones.explanation: Repeated skin sampling would have to show repair in the relevant cells and fewer accumulating mutations characteristic of ultraviolet damage. This would connect cancer prevention to the proposed repair mechanism.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm prevention, safety and persistence
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce prevention and establish safety, duration and any maintenance treatment needed. This would define which patients, cancer types and exposure conditions the protection covers.

uncertain: The repair activity, delivery method and treatment duration needed for lasting protection remain open questions.
Whether benefits extend to skin with ordinary repair, different inherited defects or transplant recipients needs separate demonstration.
Preventing new mutations may leave substantial cancer risk from mutations already present.

page.title: Epidermal DNA repair for keratinocyte cancer prevention
page.definition: An intervention increases repair of ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in the epidermis, the skin’s outer layer, and reduces new basal-cell or cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas over the intended treatment period. It may supply an enzyme that helps repair lesions such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, which link adjacent DNA bases, or restore an inherited repair defect in epidermal cells.

goal.need: An estimated 3.3 million people in the United States were treated for keratinocyte cancers in 2012. In xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), the median age at first nonmelanoma skin cancer was 9 years, compared with 67 in the general population. Sun protection limits further ultraviolet damage. Repair could act on damage already present and spare patients repeated operations if fewer tumors develop. People with XP would still need sun protection and regular skin examinations.

completion.title: FDA approves an epidermal DNA-repair therapy to prevent new keratinocyte cancers.
completion.criterion: FDA approves a new drug application or issues a biologics license for an epidermal DNA-repair therapy whose approved labeling includes prevention of new basal-cell carcinomas, cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas, or both. The approved indication and regimen define the population, cancer types and conditions of use.
completion.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 314.105(c) for new drug approval, 21 CFR 601.4(a) for biologics licensure and 21 CFR 201.57(c)(2) for the labeled indication.
completion.threshold_quote: the drug is indicated for the treatment, prevention, mitigation, cure, or diagnosis of a recognized disease or condition
completion.basis: The approved prevention indication supplies the decision rule for the cancer types and population it covers. A trial aimed at actinic keratoses can reach phase 3 before a cancer-prevention indication is established. FDA lists liposome-encapsulated T4 endonuclease V as designated for preventing cutaneous neoplasms in XP and unapproved for that indication.

milestones.criterion: In the intended population, a controlled study of an epidermal DNA-repair therapy provides preliminary evidence of a lower incidence of new basal-cell carcinomas, cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas, or both, over a specified observation period. The study characterizes common short-term adverse effects and risks.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, controlled efficacy studies in 21 CFR 312.21(b) and the evidence preceding phase 3 in 21 CFR 312.21(c).
milestones.threshold_quote: preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained

milestones.title: Confirmatory studies establish an epidermal DNA-repair drug's prevention benefit and safety.
milestones.criterion: Expanded clinical studies characterize prevention of new basal-cell or cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas and adverse effects sufficiently to assess overall benefit and risk and support prescribing information for the proposed population and regimen. The efficacy evidence includes adequate and well-controlled investigations that permit a quantitative comparison with a control.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Phase 3 objectives in 21 CFR 312.21(c) and efficacy-investigation criteria in 21 CFR 314.126.
milestones.threshold_quote: a valid comparison with a control to provide a quantitative assessment of drug effect

milestones.title: Treatment increases repair of ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in human epidermal cells.
milestones.criterion: After matched ultraviolet exposure, treated human keratinocytes or reconstructed epidermis show greater removal of a measured DNA lesion than the control at the same time after exposure, or greater repair-associated DNA synthesis where that assay measures the repair mechanism.
milestones.set_by: Experimental convention in human epidermal repair studies using lesion clearance or unscheduled DNA synthesis after ultraviolet exposure.
milestones.threshold_quote: enhanced repair synthesis in both normal and xeroderma pigmentosum keratinocytes

not_found: Searches of FDA regulations and guidance found no epidermal DNA-repair-specific minimum cancer reduction or treatment duration.
The supplied 2025 systematic review's publisher text was blocked, and the supplied NIH RePORTER page returned only a JavaScript shell.

results.finding: In 19 XPC-corrected keratinocyte clones sampled from one XP-C donor culture, no specific retroviral integration event showed clonal selection.
results.detail: The clonal selection assessment used serially propagated cells in vitro. The authors identified long-term tumorigenesis as a question for further study.
results.quote: Since these integration sites were associated with different events at each time point, we concluded that no particular integration event was clonally selected.

results.finding: In 28 patients with actinic keratosis, skin-biopsy cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers fell 61% from baseline with sunscreen plus repair enzymes.
results.detail: The biopsy measurements capture net lesion burden over six months. Without matched UV exposure, the study cannot isolate increased repair from differences in lesion formation.
results.quote: At 6 months, CPDs decreased by 61% in the enzyme group and by 35% in the sunscreen group compared with baseline values (P < 0.001).

results.finding: Among 28 randomized patients with actinic keratosis, topical sunscreen plus repair enzymes reduced skin-biopsy cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers by 61%.
results.detail: The report describes one enzyme-containing regimen and gives no enzyme dose, dose-response data, or safety results.
results.quote: At 6 months, CPDs decreased by 61% in the enzyme group and by 35% in the sunscreen group compared with baseline values (P < 0.001).

results.finding: In 30 patients with xeroderma pigmentosum, topical T4N5 reduced the annualised rate of new basal-cell carcinomas by 1.6 versus placebo.
results.detail: The analysis was by intention to treat. One placebo patient withdrew before treatment and another withdrew at nine months with progressive disease.
results.quote: For basal-cell carcinoma, the annualised rates of new lesions were 3.8 in the treatment group and 5.4 in the placebo group (difference 1.6 [0.38-2.82]).

results.quote:
However, topical SS + photolyase prevented CPD forma-
tion by ~93%, and was thus better than SS alone (P<0.001).

results.finding: Afamelanotide-treated UV-exposed human skin showed lower DNA damage markers (p<0.01). The lesion-analysis sample size is unstated.
results.detail: The seven-person sample size applies to RNA sequencing. A lower lesion signal alone cannot distinguish greater lesion removal from reduced initial lesion formation.
results.quote:
DNA-
damage markers such as γH2AX and cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers³ had been significantly reduced 
(p<0.01).

results.finding: In seven fair-skinned volunteers, afamelanotide reduced the number of UV-responsive differentially expressed genes by a factor of 3.4.
results.quote:
With 
afamelanotide, the DEGs between irradiated versus non-irradiated skin reduced to 183, a factor 3.4 less DEGs 
(p<0.05).

results.finding: Oral nicotinamide reduced UV-induced skin immunosuppression versus placebo in 59 healthy adults across two crossover studies (P<0.001 for each regimen).
results.detail: The 30 and 31 dose-cohort enrollments represent 59 unique adults. The Mantoux response measures local skin immunity, and the blood NAD assay measures a systemic response. The authors left DNA photolesion formation and repair for future experiments.
results.quote:
Repeated measures of analysis of variance showed that the DEI with
nicotinamide was signiﬁcantly different to that with placebo
(P , 0.001) for all three doses of ssUV and for each of the two doses
of nicotinamide tested.

results.finding: Among 74 adults with actinic keratoses, oral nicotinamide yielded an adjusted relative rate of 0.24 for new basal-cell or cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas over 4 months versus placebo.
results.detail: Actinic keratosis count was the primary endpoint. Cancer incidence was assessed in an unplanned pooled analysis that reported 37 participants per arm, although 76 were enrolled across the two trials.
results.quote:
During the 4-month trials, 11 placebo
patients developed 20 new skin cancers
(12 basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and
8 SCC) and 2 nicotinamide patients
developed 4 cancers (2 BCC and
2 SCC).

results.finding: Photoreactivated HaCaT human keratinocytes had 90% fewer CPDs than dark controls across three independent experiments.
results.quote: The amount of CPDs in CPD-PL Ψ-mRNA transfected cells was reduced by 90% in those receiving photoreactivating light (photoreactivated), as compared to cells kept in the dark (non-photoreactivated)

definition = "An intervention increases repair of ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in the epidermis, the skin\u2019s outer layer, and reduces new basal-cell or cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas over the intended treatment period. It may supply an enzyme that helps repair lesions such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, which link adjacent DNA bases, or restore an inherited repair defect in epidermal cells.". Reason: “Maintains removal” leaves the change in repair activity unclear and gives no example of the DNA damage being repaired.

goal.need = "An estimated 3.3 million people in the United States were treated for keratinocyte cancers in 2012. In xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), the median age at first nonmelanoma skin cancer was 9 years, compared with 67 in the general population. Sun protection limits further ultraviolet damage. Repair could act on damage already present and spare patients repeated operations if fewer tumors develop. People with XP would still need sun protection and regular skin examinations.". Reason: The age comparison shows the burden in XP but omits the wider treatment burden, the limits of sun protection and the operations patients could avoid.

add statement by National Cancer Institute, phase 2 trial NCT00089180, 2004: "Compare the incidence of nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) (average per patient)". Reason: The National Cancer Institute protocol documents a prevention goal in kidney transplant recipients that the existing statements omit.

edit completion: title = "FDA approves an epidermal DNA-repair therapy to prevent new keratinocyte cancers."; criterion = "FDA approves a new drug application or issues a biologics license for an epidermal DNA-repair therapy whose approved labeling includes prevention of new basal-cell carcinomas, cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas, or both. The approved indication and regimen define the population, cancer types and conditions of use."; set_by = "U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 314.105(c) for new drug approval, 21 CFR 601.4(a) for biologics licensure and 21 CFR 201.57(c)(2) for the labeled indication."; set_by_kind = "regulator"; threshold_quote = "the drug is indicated for the treatment, prevention, mitigation, cure, or diagnosis of a recognized disease or condition"; threshold_ref = 23; basis = "The approved prevention indication supplies the decision rule for the cancer types and population it covers. A trial aimed at actinic keratoses can reach phase 3 before a cancer-prevention indication is established. FDA lists liposome-encapsulated T4 endonuclease V as designated for preventing cutaneous neoplasms in XP and unapproved for that indication."; refs = [4, 22, 23, 24, 25]. Reason: The existing test cites only new drug approval despite including genetic correction, for which biologics licensure can supply the marketing decision.

add milestone after None: "Treatment increases repair of ultraviolet-induced DNA damage in human epidermal cells.". Reason: Increased repair in epidermal cells can be demonstrated before there is enough toxicology evidence to support human dosing.

edit m1: criterion = "Pharmacology and toxicology studies in laboratory animals or in vitro provide an adequate basis for the sponsor to conclude that the proposed human investigation is reasonably safe. The nature and duration of the proposed investigation determine the kind, duration and scope of testing."; threshold_quote = "it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations."; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5]. Reason: The skin-explant and mouse findings are individual results, while the FDA criterion concerns the evidence supporting the safety of the proposed human study.

edit m2: criterion = "Human dosing characterizes tolerability, acute adverse effects and pharmacological activity. The information on dose and drug effects is sufficient to design a well-controlled phase 2 study."; set_by = "U.S. Food and Drug Administration, phase 1 objectives in 21 CFR 312.21(a) and Step 3: Clinical Research."; threshold_quote = "how much of a drug the body can tolerate and what its acute side effects are."; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 10]. edit m3: title = "Controlled studies show preliminary prevention of new basal-cell or cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas."; criterion = "In the intended population, a controlled study of an epidermal DNA-repair therapy provides preliminary evidence of a lower incidence of new basal-cell carcinomas, cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas, or both, over a specified observation period.
